title: Choreography and Motion Mapping
answer: Kinematic generation, notation, motion capture retargeting, crowd simulation and biomechanics.

children.name: Kinematic Video and Generated Movement
children.blurb: Kinematic video and generated movement covers systems that record, analyse, and synthesise human or animal motion for choreography, animation, and performance.

children.name: Dance Notation and Transcription
children.blurb: Dance notation and transcription in this context covers the capture of human movement and its conversion into a readable, repeatable symbolic form, such as Labanotation or Benesh Movement Notation.

children.name: Motion Capture and Retargeting
children.blurb: Motion capture and retargeting covers recording human movement from sensors or video and mapping that movement onto a different body or character.

children.name: Crowd and Ensemble Simulation
children.blurb: Crowd and ensemble simulation covers the computational generation and coordination of movement for multiple performers or background figures, from large battle scenes and stadium crowds to small dance ensembles.

children.name: Biomechanical Analysis
children.blurb: Biomechanical analysis in choreography and motion mapping uses AI to measure and interpret human movement, from joint angles and muscle activation to balance and force.

sections.body: This field applies machine learning to how bodies and groups move, from generating new movement sequences to recording and transferring existing ones. Kinematic video and generated movement use models trained on motion data to produce short clips of human or animal motion, often for previz, dance, or synthetic media. Dance notation and transcription work on converting recorded movement into structured scores or text, and sometimes back into animation. Motion capture and retargeting take performances from sensors or video and map them onto different body shapes or characters. Crowd and ensemble simulation models how many moving figures interact, while biomechanical analysis measures joint angles, forces, and patterns for study rather than performance.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work is uneven. Kinematic generation can produce plausible short motions but often fails on long sequences, contact with objects, and unusual body types. Dance notation systems are partially automated for common steps, but full transcription from video remains unreliable, especially for fast or occluded movement. Motion capture retargeting is mature for studio conditions with markers, but markerless capture from ordinary video still drifts and loses detail. Crowd simulation handles large groups with simple rules well, yet realistic individual behavior within a crowd is not solved. Biomechanical analysis can estimate some joint angles from video, but accurate force and muscle data still require physical sensors or lab setups, and the site's count of 1000 live video models shows only a small portion are built for motion rather than general video.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: A reader interested in how new movement is created should start with Kinematic Video and Generated Movement, which covers the generative side. Dance Notation and Transcription connects that output to formal systems like Labanotation, useful for preservation or analysis. Motion Capture and Retargeting is the bridge between real performance and digital characters, and it feeds both the generative and notation pages with clean motion data. Crowd and Ensemble Simulation extends single body motion to groups, which matters for scenes with many dancers or background figures. Biomechanical Analysis sits at the measurement end, providing the physical constraints and data that the other pages rely on when they need realistic or safe movement. Together they move from generation to recording to transfer to groups to physical measurement.
